title: The Other
subtitle: Only one other living person comes to the House. He is polite, helpful and always in a hurry. How do you decide whether to trust someone who is the only person you know?

card.who: Susanna Clarke · Piranesi · trust, kindness and control
card.essence: A man who depends on one visitor for everything he knows about the world. How to read what people say, what they do and what it costs them.

intention: you'll talk about trust, helpfulness and control, use a four-step check for deciding how far to believe someone, and practise the language of reading between the lines.
warmup: Think of someone who was helpful to you but whom you slowly stopped trusting. What changed?
What do you look at first when you decide whether to believe someone: what they say, what they do, or how they say it?
Can a person be kind and controlling at the same time? Give an example.

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: He was always courteous to the staff, thanking them and holding the door, even when he was in a hurry.
When she asked where he had been, he gave an evasive answer and changed the subject.
items.meaning: evasive (adjective) — deliberately avoiding giving a direct answer. Verb: evade.

items.sent: Some people manipulate others by being very kind at first and then asking for favours.
items.meaning: manipulate (verb) — to control or influence someone cleverly or unfairly, often without their noticing. Noun: manipulation.

items.sent: A small suspicion grew into a firm belief that something was being hidden from her.
items.meaning: suspicion (noun) — a feeling that someone has done something wrong, or that something is not as it seems. Verb: suspect.

vocab.heading: B · Which term means…?
vocab.intro: Three terms: read between the lines · take at face value · keep an eye on. Say the right one, then reveal.

items.sent: Which term means to understand a meaning that is not stated openly?
items.meaning: read between the lines — If you read between the lines, the letter is a warning.

items.sent: Which term means to accept something exactly as it appears, without looking for a deeper meaning?
items.meaning: take at face value — She took his offer at face value and did not ask why.

items.sent: Which term means to watch someone or something carefully because you are not sure about them?
items.meaning: keep an eye on — Keep an eye on the figures; they may change.

vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: earn someone's ___  ·  break ___  ·  a relationship built on ___
items.meaning: trust — a firm belief that someone is honest and reliable.

items.sent: a hidden ___  ·  an ulterior ___  ·  question someone's ___
items.meaning: motive — a reason for doing something, especially a hidden or selfish one.

items.sent: set the ___  ·  a friendly ___  ·  change your ___

When did you read between the lines and find a message nobody had stated?

story_heading: One visitor, one version of the world

story.heading: Part 1 — The only visitor
paras: For the narrator, the Other is not only a person. He is the connection to everything outside the narrator's own routine. He brings small supplies and news of the search he is engaged in, and he tells Piranesi what is useful, what is not, and what he should or should not do.
The Other is courteous, but there is something slightly cold under the courtesy. He gives instructions as if they were requests. He seems pleased when Piranesi is cheerful and puzzled when he is not.
The narrator describes him fairly and with obvious respect. It takes the reader some time to ask whether that respect has been earned.
answers: Small supplies, news of his search, and advice on what Piranesi should do.
Courteous, but slightly cold; he gives instructions as if they were requests.
Whether the narrator's respect for him has been earned.
story.discuss: Think of a relationship in which one person decides what the other needs to know. How can you tell when it is helpful and when it is control?

story.heading: Part 2 — Small signs
paras: Little things begin to accumulate. The Other's explanations are tidy, perhaps too tidy. He answers some questions at length and avoids others. He worries aloud about Piranesi's health and sometimes says that he is not quite himself, which has the effect of making Piranesi doubt his own judgement.

The narrator notices this in his own way. He does not accuse anyone. He records, compares and waits. What changes is the kind of question he writes in his notes: not only what happened but who told him so.
This is the point at which the book becomes a quiet kind of thriller. Nothing explodes. The tension comes from tone and from the gap between what is said and what is done.
checks: How does the Other answer questions?
What does he say about Piranesi's health?
Where does the tension come from?
answers: At length on some, and he avoids others.
That Piranesi is not quite himself, which makes him doubt his own judgement.
From tone, and from the gap between what is said and what is done.
story.discuss: Have you ever been told you were not quite yourself by someone who gained from your doubt? How did you decide what to believe?

story.heading: Part 3 — Choosing whom to believe
paras: Eventually signs appear that the Other is not the only person in the House, and the narrator has to choose between competing accounts of who is trustworthy. He does not simply swap one belief for another. He tests things in small ways, watches what people do and compares it with what they said.

That, in the end, is the book's idea of trust: not a feeling but a habit of paying attention. It also makes the novel a good one to discuss in a group, because readers disagree about how much the narrator should have noticed and when.
Whichever side you take, it is worth asking what exactly made you trust or distrust each person, and how soon.
checks: What does the narrator do when he has to choose?
What is the book's idea of trust?
Why is it good to discuss in a group?
answers: He tests things in small ways and compares what people do with what they said.
Not a feeling but a habit of paying attention.
Because readers disagree about how much he should have noticed and when.
story.discuss: At what point did you start to trust or distrust each person in the book? What was the first thing that changed your mind?

tool_tab.lead: You can use the same habit the narrator develops. The Trust Check is a loop of four moves for deciding how far to believe someone: listen to what they say, watch what they do, ask what it costs them, and test a small thing.
how: Listen: note exactly what was said, not what you assumed. He said it would take a week.
Watch: compare it with what happens. It has now taken a month, and he has not mentioned it.
Ask what it costs them: who gains if you believe this, and who loses? If I believe him, he keeps control of the schedule.
Test: check one small thing that you can verify. If it holds, trust a little more. If not, trust a little less. Never decide on one test.

sort.intro: Each sentence describes something a person might do in a relationship of trust. Which move of the Trust Check does it belong to?

items.text: I wrote down exactly what she promised, word for word.
I noticed that he agreed to everything but never did any of it.
items.why: it compares what is said with what is done.

items.text: I asked myself who would benefit if I believed the story.
items.why: it looks for the interest behind the words.

items.text: I checked one small fact he had given me, to see if it was true.
She says she is busy, but her calendar was empty.
What was the exact wording he used about the date?
items.why: it focuses on what was actually said.

items.text: If I agree, will he gain anything from it, and what will I lose?
Let me ask a question whose answer I already know.
items.why: a simple way to check reliability.

breaks: Do not become a detective in every relationship. Most people most of the time deserve a little trust. Use the check when something does not add up.
One test is not enough. A single lie can be a mistake; a pattern is information.
Your own motives matter too. Sometimes we want to believe, or to doubt. Ask what you want to be true.
discuss: Which move do you tend to skip, and what has it cost you?
Is it possible to trust someone and also check what they say?

grammar.name: Reading between the lines
grammar.lead: To talk about what is implied and not stated, English has a handful of structures that make careful, polite and precise judgements.
notes: Reporting what people imply: He implied that she was not well. She suggested that the plan had changed. It sounded as if he was hiding something. Use imply, suggest, hint for meanings that are not stated.
Hedging your own judgement: It may be that he was trying to help. Perhaps he simply did not know. I get the impression that he was not telling the whole story. The hedge keeps your claim fair.
Contrast for tone: He was polite, but there was something cold in it. Although he sounded kind, he never answered the question. Use but, although, yet to hold two readings together.

exercises.heading: Choose the verb
exercises.intro: Complete each sentence with the best verb from the box. Use each once: implied · suggested · hinted · sounded.
items: 1. She never said it directly, but she ___ that he should leave.
2. It ___ as if he was hiding something.
3. He ___ at a problem without saying what it was.
4. The report ___ that the figures had been changed.

exercises.heading: Soften the claim
exercises.intro: Rewrite each sentence with the hedge in brackets.
items: 1. He was lying. (I get the impression that)
2. She wanted to help. (It may be that)
4. He seemed kind. He ignored her question. (although)
answers: 1. I get the impression that he was lying.
2. It may be that she wanted to help.
4. Although he seemed kind, he ignored her question.

grammar.closing: Now describe someone you do not fully trust, in four sentences. Use one implied or suggested, one hedge and one although.

speak.intro: Choose a task, start the timer and talk. On your own it works as a talk; with a partner or a group, take turns and respond to each other.
speak.useful: “I get the impression that…” · “It may be that…” · “What he did was different from what he said.” · “Although he sounded kind…” · “I would want to check…”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Whom would you trust?
paras: Think of the people in the book. Whom would you have trusted at the start, and why? Use the Trust Check to explain.

tasks.label: Task 2 — The check in real life
paras: Think of a recent decision where you had to decide whether to believe someone, a salesperson, a colleague, a website. Take us through the four moves.

tasks.label: Task 3 — Kind and controlling
paras: Describe a person you know, or one from a book or a film, who is kind and controlling at the same time. How can you tell? Where would you draw the line?

final: Is it better to trust too much or too little? Why?
The narrator accepts a lot without asking. What would you have asked first?
How can you test someone's honesty without damaging the relationship?
From memory: explain the Trust Check in five sentences, using read between the lines, motive and I get the impression that.
